title: Rates and Returns
overview: Return measures translate changes in value and cash flows into comparable performance rates.
example: Work from a small return series, state the assumptions, calculate the measure, and explain what the number leaves out.

modules.title: Interest Rates and Return Measurement
modules.explanation: A holding-period return combines income with the change in price relative to the starting value. Annualization makes periods comparable, while real, leveraged, and after-tax returns reveal how inflation, financing, and taxes change the investor's result.
steps: Write beginning value, ending value, and distributions with consistent signs.

formula.label: Required return
formula.expression: r = real risk-free rate + inflation premium + risk premiums
formula.interpretation: Each premium compensates the investor for a distinct source of risk.
formula.example: A 2% real rate, 3% expected inflation, and 1.5% combined risk premiums imply an approximate required return of 6.5%.

modules.title: Time-Weighted and Money-Weighted Returns
modules.explanation: Time-weighted return removes the effect of external cash-flow timing, while money-weighted return is the discount rate that makes an investor's dated cash flows balance. They answer different questions, so the cash-flow timeline determines which measure is appropriate.
steps: Place every contribution, withdrawal, and ending value on a timeline.
Use linked subperiod returns for manager performance; use an internal rate of return for the investor experience.
Check the sign and timing of each cash flow before interpreting the result.

formula.label: Holding-period return
formula.expression: HPR = (ending value + income − beginning value) / beginning value
formula.interpretation: Include distributions received during the measurement period.
formula.example: A position bought for 100, sold for 106, and paying 2 has an 8% holding-period return.
